title: feat: web search, fetch, and citation UI
description:
## Summary

When a chat response cites web search/fetch results, users currently have
to parse inline citation text to know what was referenced. This PR renders
each citation as a compact aside pill next to the claim it supports, and
adds a single "Sources" pill per message that aggregates every citation
in that message so users can scan all sources at a glance without hunting
through the response.

This is built on top of #278's generic `<shiny-aside>` markup convention —
citations are just asides tagged with a `data-citation` marker, so as that
component evolves (interaction handling, styling, etc.) citations should
keep working without changes here. This PR stacks on #278 and will need
to be rebased once it merges.

## What's included

- Web search/fetch tool activity (query, results, fetch status) rendered
  as UI onto the shiny-aside base
- Citations deduped per message (same URL + rendered body only shown once)
- A message-scoped collector aggregates citations from all asides in a
  message into a "Sources" pill + popover, with favicons and titles
- Test coverage: unit (citation model/collector), component
  (SourcesSummary, dedupe plugin), and Playwright e2e

## Python only, for now — R is blocked on ellmer

The server-side half of this (chatlas web search/fetch/citation content →
`<shiny-web-search>` / `<shiny-web-fetch>` / `<shiny-aside data-citation>`
markup) currently only ships for Python. Porting it to R's `contents_shinychat()`
is blocked on gaps in ellmer 0.4.2:

- `ContentToolRequestSearch` / `ContentToolResponseSearch` / `ContentToolRequestFetch` /
  `ContentToolResponseFetch` exist in ellmer but aren't exported, so there's no
  public way to hook `contents_shinychat()` onto them.
- `ContentToolResponseSearch` only carries bare URLs, no titles.
- `ContentToolResponseFetch` has no normalized success/error status.
- Citations aren't a first-class content type in ellmer at all — they're parsed
  during streaming and then dropped when the final `ContentText` is built, so
  there's nothing to hook inline citation rendering onto.

None of this is filed upstream yet. Until it lands, R support for this feature
is a documented gap rather than something worked around with unexported-internals
access or provider-specific JSON parsing inside shinychat.

## Test plan

- [ ] `cd js && npm run lint && npm test`
- [ ] `uv run pytest` (Playwright web_citations suite)
- [ ] Manual: ask a chatlas-backed app to do a web search, confirm inline
      citation pills dedupe and the Sources pill lists all of them

title: fix(pkg-r): faithfully restore displayed chat UI from bookmark, not re-derived turns
description:
## Why

#272 made the browser the authoritative source for what a chat currently
displays, so the server always saves the exact rendered snapshot the user
saw (transformations included) rather than re-deriving it from LLM turns.

`chat_restore()` never got the other half of that: on restore, it still
called `client_set_ui()`, which regenerates the UI straight from the
`client`'s turns. Any transformation applied between receiving a message
and displaying it (custom rendering, markdown post-processing, etc.) was
silently dropped on restore, even though the browser's own snapshot -
the thing #272 introduced - had it the whole time. Bookmark restoration
and live chat state also disagreed about what "the chat" looked like.

There was a second, related gap: the "bookmark on response" trigger fired
when the assistant's stream completed, but the browser echoes its settled
message snapshot back to the server in a later round trip. Bookmarking
on stream completion could persist a snapshot missing the reply that had
just finished, since the browser hadn't reported it yet.

## What changed

- `chat_restore()` now captures the browser's reported message snapshot
  into the bookmark's `state$values` (server bookmark store only - the
  gzip+base64 payload isn't URL-bookmark friendly) and replays that
  snapshot on restore, preserving display-only transformations exactly
  as shown.
- Falls back to the old turn-derived `client_set_ui()` path for
  `bookmarkStore = "url"` and for bookmarks saved before this snapshot
  existed, so nothing breaks for existing bookmarks.
- The "bookmark on response" observer now fires off the client's
  `_messages` echo (once it reports a settled transcript ending in an
  assistant message), instead of stream completion - mirroring the same
  fix #272 already made for history saves, applied here to bookmarks.
- Guards the response-bookmark trigger against firing during initial UI
  population (a fresh session's pre-seeded turns, or a restore itself) -
  only a genuine user-submitted exchange should mint an automatic
  bookmark.
- Fixes a separate cross-R-version bug in bookmark/UI-snapshot
  decompression, and removes bookmark-on-response code made fully dead
  by the trigger change above.
- Adds `encode_ui_snapshot()`/`decode_ui_snapshot()` (reusing the
  `serializeJSON` -> gzip -> base64 pipeline already used for client
  state) plus regression tests covering round-tripping, htmlDeps/
  attachments preservation, and the fallback path for pre-snapshot
  bookmarks.

## Test plan

- [x] New testthat coverage for snapshot encode/decode, faithful replay,
      and turn-derived fallback (`pkg-r/tests/testthat/test-chat_restore.R`)
- [x] `devtools::test()` / `devtools::check()` in `pkg-r/` — 599 passed, 0 failures

title: feat: <shiny-sidenote> markup for source pills + popovers
description:
## Why this matters Assistant responses increasingly need to *cite their sources* — a web search result, a fetched page, a methodology note — without derailing the prose. This PR adds a general-purpose way to do exactly that: drop an inline `` tag anywhere in a message's markdown and it renders as a small **pill** at the end of the paragraph (or list item) it belongs to. Hover, click, or keyboard-focus the pill and a **popover** shows the note's body. The key design decision is that this is a **plain markup convention, not an API**. Any content that reaches the chat as markdown can carry these tags — hand-authored, templated, or (the intended path) emitted by an LLM you've prompted to cite its sources. There is no new Python/R function to call and nothing source-specific baked in: `Chat.append_message()` / `chat_append()` already stream markdown, and sidenotes ride along inside it. This is the rendering primitive that the upcoming **web search / web fetch citation UI** is built on top of (see "Foundation for web citations" below). ## What it looks like Sidenotes render at the **end of the block** they belong to, regardless of where in the sentence the tag was authored — the markup pass pulls each tag out of its inline position and appends the resulting pill(s) to the tail of the paragraph or list item. A labeled sidenote renders as an *identity chip* — a favicon (derived from `url`) plus the source name: ``` Hub motors are cheaper, and ideal for flatter terrain. [🌐 eBicycles] └─ end of block ─┘ hover/click/focus opens the popover ``` When several distinct sources are cited in the same block, their pills **collapse into one** — the first source becomes the face, the rest become a `+N` overflow, and the popover turns into a **carousel** with prev/next controls: ``` Hub motors are cheaper, and ideal for flatter terrain. [🌐 eBicycles +1] ┌─────────────────────────────┐ │ ‹ › 1 / 2 │ │ 🌐 eBicycles │ │ Hub Motor vs. Mid-Drive… │ └─────────────────────────────┘ ``` A sidenote with **no `label`** falls back to a plain numbered marker (`[1]`, `[2]`, … numbered across the whole message), so anonymous notes still work: ``` Battery quality matters more than raw power. [1] ``` A single block can carry **more than one pill**: all labeled sidenotes merge into one source-chip, while each label-less sidenote becomes its own numbered marker — so the tail of a paragraph might show a chip *and* a couple of numbered pills together. ## The convention ```html markdown shown in the popover ``` - The tag can be authored **anywhere in the sentence**; it always renders at the **end of its block** (paragraph or list item). - **`label`** (optional) — source name shown on the pill/chip. Sidenotes sharing a **label** within a block are grouped under one chip and paged through (prev/next) rather than deduped — every entry is kept. Without a label, the pill is a numbered marker. - **`url`** (optional) — used to derive a favicon and is URL-sanitized. - **`icon`** (optional) — overrides the favicon; also URL-sanitized. - **body** = the tag's own markdown children. Inline for a one-liner, or — separated by blank lines — a **rich block body** (paragraphs, lists, code). ### Examples Labeled, one-line body: ```python await chat.append_message( "Hub motors are cheaper" '' "[Hub Motor vs. Mid-Drive Motor Differences Explained](https://ebicycles.example/hub-vs-mid-drive)" "" ", and ideal for flatter terrain." ) ``` Two sources in one sentence collapse into a single pill: ```python "...cheaper" '…' '…' ", and ideal for flatter terrain." ``` Label-less sidenote with a rich block body (blank line ⇒ block body), falls back to a numbered pill: ```python "Battery quality matters more than raw power" "\n\n" "**Methodology**\n\n" "- 40 commuter e-bike models\n" "- released in 2024\n\n" "" ``` The same markup works in R via `chat_append()` — see the **Sidenotes** section in the `?chat_append` / `append_message()` docs for the full reference. ## Try it locally These example apps aren't part of this PR's diff (kept local, not committed) but are the easiest way to see every scenario at once.
sandbox/demo_sidenotes.py — exhaustive manual scenarios (Python, no API key needed) ```python # Exhaustive manual test of the public markup convention # (no chatlas / API key needed — this branch does not depend on it). # Run: uv run shiny run sandbox/demo_sidenotes.py --port 8054 # # Every scenario renders directly in the startup greeting — nothing to click. # Scroll the one assistant message to see: same-label paging, overflow + popover # carousel, label-less sequential numbering (message-scoped, not per-group — # see the dedicated section below), icon-without-url, missing icon/url, # special characters, tight/loose/nested lists, multi-paragraph grouping, # and a rich-markdown popover body. # # Typing a scenario name still re-sends it through append_message_stream, # streamed in small chunks — closer to how a real LLM emits tokens, and # useful for exercising the streaming-specific code path (the greeting # itself is rendered statically, not streamed). import asyncio from shiny.express import ui from shinychat.express import Chat ui.page_opts(title="shinychat — Sidenote Markup Demo", fillable=True) SCENARIOS: dict[str, str] = { "Show a single cited source": '''Tidy evaluation lets you write functions that work like dplyr data-masking semantics[Metaprogramming: Evaluation](https://adv-r.hadley.nz/evaluation.html), the tidy evaluation chapter of Advanced R..''', "Cite the same source twice": '''The de facto style guide for R is the tidyverse style guide[The tidyverse style guide](https://style.tidyverse.org), and most packages on CRAN now follow itSecond citation for the same source — should page as a second entry under the same pill, not add an overflow badge.. Expect one pill above with no overflow count, but a 2-entry prev/next carousel in the popover.''', "Cite three different sources": '''Three different benchmarks all reach the same conclusion[R-bloggers benchmark writeup](https://www.r-bloggers.com): vectorized code consistently outperforms explicit loops[Advanced R, performance chapter](https://adv-r.hadley.nz), often by an order of magnitude or more[CRAN Task View: High-Performance Computing](https://cran.r-project.org/web/views/HighPerformanceComputing.html). Expect one pill labeled "R-bloggers" with a "+2" overflow badge, and a 3-way carousel in the popover.''', "Label-less numbering, case A — one paragraph, one anonymous claim": '''Internal testing suggests this approach scales to about 40 million rows before memory becomes a bottleneckBenchmarked on a 16-core, 64GB machine using data.table with fread().. Expect a pill reading "1" (no label, no favicon; accessible name "Sidenote 1") — this is a running index scoped to the whole message, not a count of this group's entries.''', "Label-less numbering, case B — a separate paragraph, also one anonymous claim": '''A completely unrelated claim, in its own paragraph, also with a single anonymous sourceA different benchmark, on different hardware, cited independently of case A above.. Expect this pill to read "2" — continuing the running count from case A above, not resetting to "1". Anonymous sidenotes are numbered sequentially across the entire message, regardless of which paragraph or list item they land in.''', "Label-less numbering, case C — one paragraph, three anonymous claims": '''This recommendation is backed by three separate signals: internal testingTested on 500 real user sessions over two weeks., user interviews12 semi-structured interviews with power users., and support ticket analysisReviewed 200 tickets tagged performance from the last quarter.. Expect three separate pills reading "3", "4", and "5" — anonymous sidenotes are never bundled together, even within the same paragraph; each gets its own pill and its own consecutive number, continuing from case B above.''', "Label-less numbering, case D — mixing a labeled source with an anonymous claim": '''A cited claim[A public, labeled source](https://example.com/public). alongside an uncited one in the same sentenceAn anonymous claim grouped into the same paragraph as the labeled citation above.. Expect TWO separate pills: one labeled "Public Source" with no overflow badge (anonymous sidenotes never count toward a labeled pill's overflow), and one numbered pill reading "6" — continuing the running count from case C above.''', "Use a custom icon with no link": '''Model responses are graded against a private held-out benchmarkInternal evaluation suite — not publicly documented, so there is no link, only an explicit icon override.. Expect the pill to show the given icon even though no url is set.''', "Use a label with no link or icon": '''This is common knowledge among R usersNo source needed — this is a widely known fact in the R community.. Expect a labeled pill with no favicon image at all.''', "Use special characters in a citation": '''Pricing details are on the vendor site[Pricing page](https://example.com/pricing?plan=pro&ref=chat&utm_source=app) — the label and URL both contain ampersands, to check attribute escaping and link generation.. Expect the label to read "Docs & Pricing" and the popover link to point at a URL with literal & characters.''', "Cite sources in a tight list": '''Recommended reading, in order of depth:\n\n- Start with the official docs[Official documentation](https://docs.example.com)\n- Then this in-depth guide[An in-depth guide](https://guide.example.com)\n- Finally, the source code itself[Source repository](https://github.com/example/repo)\n\nExpect each list item to carry its own single-source pill.''', "Cite sources in a loose list": '''Three separate, independently-sourced points:\n\n- Point one, well substantiated[Source A](https://a.example.com)\n\n- Point two, also cited[Source B](https://b.example.com)\n\n- Point three, no citation needed here\n\nBlank lines between items force a loose list (each item wrapped in its own paragraph) — expect the same per-item pills as the tight-list case.''', "Cite sources in a nested list": '''- Outer point, cited directly[Outer source](https://outer.example.com)\n - Nested sub-point with its own citation[Inner source](https://inner.example.com) — must attach to the nested item, not the outer one.\n\nExpect two separate pills: one on the outer bullet, one on the nested bullet — neither should steal the other sidenote.''', "Cite sources in separate paragraphs": '''First, consider the frontend[Frontend guide](https://frontend.example.com).\n\nNow consider the backend[Backend guide](https://backend.example.com).\n\nExpect two separate pills, one per paragraph.''', "Show a rich-text popover body": '''Full details are in the changelogReleased **v2.4.0** with a new `parallel=` argument and a [full changelog here](https://changelog.example.com). See also *migration notes* below.. Expect the popover body to render bold, italic, inline code, and a link — not raw markdown syntax.''', } GREETING = "## Sidenote markup scenarios\n\n" + "\n\n".join( f"**{name}**\n\n{content}" for name, content in SCENARIOS.items() ) chat = Chat(id="chat") chat.ui( greeting=GREETING, placeholder="Type a scenario name above to re-stream it in chunks…", ) async def stream_chunks(text: str, chunk_size: int = 10): # Small chunk_size + a visible delay means a tag almost # always lands split across multiple chunks, and slow enough to watch the # incomplete opening tag get hidden until the tag (and its sidenote) # fully arrives. for i in range(0, len(text), chunk_size): yield text[i : i + chunk_size] await asyncio.sleep(0.08) @chat.on_user_submit async def _(user_input: str): content = SCENARIOS.get(user_input.strip()) if content is None: options = "\n".join(f"- {name}" for name in SCENARIOS) await chat.append_message( f"Not a recognized scenario. Try one of:\n\n{options}" ) return await chat.append_message_stream(stream_chunks(content)) ```
## Feature checklist - ✅ Inline `` tag anywhere in a block → trailing pill at end-of-block - ✅ Labeled → favicon + name chip; label-less → message-scoped numbered marker - ✅ Multiple sources per block collapse into one pill with a `+N` overflow and a prev/next carousel popover; anonymous notes stay as separate numbered pills - ✅ Sidenotes sharing a `label` within a block page through every entry (prev/next) instead of deduping; the `+N` overflow badge is shown only for mixed-label groups, since paging already conveys the same-label count - ✅ Popover body is real markdown — inline **or** block-level (lists, code, paragraphs) - ✅ Opens on hover / click (pin) / keyboard focus; Escape and click-outside dismiss; rendered through a floating-ui portal so it escapes the message list's scroll container (flips/shifts into view instead of clipping) - ✅ **Streaming-aware**: a pill in the still-open trailing block stays hidden until its block settles (a later block starts, or the stream ends), so it doesn't flash mid-sentence or jitter as text streams past; an incomplete `` yet). Both stop a partially-arrived tag from flashing as raw text mid-stream. 3. **Inline markup convention → rehype restructuring → rendered form.** Both are conventions the LLM emits inline that a rehype pass rewrites into something richer. **Key distinction:** suggestions *promote in place* (the list stays where it sits, just restructured), whereas sidenotes *relocate to end-of-block*. The shared DNA is the streaming/finalization plumbing, not the placement semantics. ## Foundation for web search / web fetch citation UI This is deliberately the **substrate** for the citations work, not the whole thing. Once chatlas surfaces web-search/fetch results and citations during a stream, shinychat can normalize each citation into a `` — label = source title, url = source URL, body = the cited snippet — and get the pill / dedupe / carousel / streaming behavior *for free*, with no citation-specific rendering component. Because it's just markup, the same mechanism covers hand-authored notes and any other "attach a source to this sentence" use case. The `Sidenote` component keeps a null-render fallback so a stray/ungrouped carrier from that pipeline degrades silently rather than leaking a raw custom element. ## Implementation notes (for reviewers) The heavy lifting is a set of rehype passes wired into both the markdown and HTML processors (`js/src/markdown/processors.ts`): - **`rewriteSidenoteTemplate`** — round-trips `` through a `

title: fix: resolve race between the chat greeting and history restore
description:
## Problem

When both a greeting and chat history are enabled, the greeting could show at the wrong time.

- Reloading a page that restores an existing conversation would briefly flash the app's greeting before the restored transcript replaced it.
- Starting a new chat in a session that *began* by restoring an existing conversation would never show a greeting again for the rest of that session.

**To reproduce (before this fix):**
```python
Chat(
    id="chat",
    client=my_client,
    greeting=chat_greeting("## Welcome!", persistent=True),
    history=HistoryOptions(...),
)
```
1. Load the app, send a message (this saves a conversation).
2. Reload the page — the conversation restores, but the greeting flashes briefly first.
3. Open the history drawer and click "New chat" — no greeting ever appears again this session.

## Root cause

The greeting used to resolve via an independent client-side signal (`{id}_greeting_requested`, which fires whenever the chat is visible, empty, and has no greeting) that raced the server's async history-restore decision. Whichever finished first determined the (inconsistent) outcome.

## Fix

Greeting resolution now defers to the same "is this conversation restored?" decision `HistoryController` already computes — once at startup, and now also on every `new_chat()` — instead of racing the client's independent request:

- `HistoryController.replay_ui()` (used both on initial restore and when switching conversations from the drawer) now explicitly clears any greeting, since a restored conversation is never a "new chat".
- `HistoryController.new_chat()` now re-resolves the greeting directly, so a fresh conversation always gets one — even in a session that began by restoring an existing conversation.

Applied symmetrically in `pkg-py` and `pkg-r`.

## Testing

- New Playwright e2e coverage: no greeting flash on restore, greeting clears when switching to an old conversation, and greeting reappears after "New chat" in a session that started by restoring a conversation.
- Unit tests for the new `HistoryController.on_settled`/`notify_settled` hook in both languages.
- Existing greeting e2e tests were switched to use `persistent=True` greetings — a plain-string greeting is auto-dismissed by the client regardless of this fix, so those tests passed even against the buggy code (a false negative).

title: feat(r): standalone register_slash_command()
description:
Fixes the standing `TODO` in `chat_app.R` for a standalone `register_slash_command()`. See #273 for motivation and the proposed API.

## What this does

Factors the slash-command registration machinery out of `chat_server()` into:

- **`register_slash_command(id, name, description, handler, ..., echo = NULL, force = FALSE, session = getDefaultReactiveDomain())`** — exported. A free function you can call from anywhere with just the chat `id` and `session`; no need to thread `chat_server()`'s return value, and it works with a fully custom `chat_ui()` + `chat_append()` loop (no `chat_server()` required).
- **`slash_commands_registry(id, session)`** — internal. Get-or-create the per-`(session, id)` command registry, wiring the dispatch + sync observers exactly once. State lives in `session$userData` keyed by the namespaced id, matching the `chat_restore.R` idiom.

`chat_server()`'s `$slash_command()` is now a thin wrapper over `register_slash_command()`, so **both paths share one implementation**. This is a pure refactor — no behavior change to the existing `chat_server()` API.

## Semantics (unchanged from `$slash_command()`)

- `handler`: 0-/1-arg function, or `NULL` for client-side handling via the cancelable `shiny:chat-slash-command` event. A 1-arg handler receives a `ContentSlashCommand`.
- `echo` defaults to `TRUE` when a handler is supplied, `FALSE` otherwise.
- `force` overwrites an existing command; returns an unregister function.
- Argument order follows `chat_append()` / `chat_clear()` (`id` first, `session` last).

## Test plan

- [x] Existing `chat_server` slash tests still pass (updated the 3 that reached into the old closure to read the registry from its new location).
- [x] New `register_slash_command()` tests: 0-/1-arg dispatch, `ContentSlashCommand` payload, validation, `echo` defaults, `force`, unregister, single-registry-per-`(session, id)`.
- [x] Full suite green (`devtools::test()`, 516 tests, 0 failures).
- [x] `R CMD check`: 0 errors, 0 warnings (remaining NOTES are pre-existing and unrelated).
- [x] Verified end-to-end in a real headless browser: the palette renders and commands dispatch for both `chat_server()` and standalone `register_slash_command()`, including inside a Shiny module, the 0-arg path, the client-side `NULL`-handler + `preventDefault()` path, and the `content@text` → `chat_append()` pattern.

## Open question

I kept the unregister-closure return (R idiom). If you'd rather have a `remove_slash_command()` for parity with Python's `Chat.remove_slash_command()`, I'm happy to add it.

title: feat: make the browser the source of truth for chat messages
description:
<!-- Title options (pick one) -->
<!-- A: feat: make the browser the source of truth for chat messages (Python + R) -->
<!-- B: feat: restore chat conversations as displayed, not as the LLM emitted them (Python + R) -->


Faithfully saving and restoring a conversation means tracking two things: the
**LLM-facing state** (the turns to and from the model) and the **user-facing
state** (what's actually displayed). They aren't always the same — apps can
transform a response in a way that isn't (or shouldn't be) visible to the LLM 
or shinychat.

Now that the UI runs on React, the user-facing state already lives in the
client. This PR leans into that: instead of the server tracking displayed
messages on its own, the browser reports its state and the server treats it as
authoritative — one mechanism shared by both R and Python.

## What changes

- **The client reports its rendered messages.** The React app sends a
  settled-message snapshot to the server as a new `${id}_messages` input; the
  server reads that as the record of the user-facing conversation.
- **Python** already tracked user-facing state, but in a separate server-side
  accumulator (`_messages` / `_store_message`) — a redundant copy of what the
  browser holds. That's removed; `.messages()`, bookmark serialization, and
  history now read the client's report. History's save-idempotency guard drops
  its two replay-suppression flags for a simpler count-based check.
- **R** never tracked user-facing state, so its history (#266) restored
  straight from turns and lost every transformation. It gains the same protocol
  and now restores the exact displayed message, falling back to turn-derived
  markdown only for conversations captured before this change.

## Why this is better

- **R and Python history now share one model.** Previously each answered "what
  did the user see?" differently — Python kept a server-side accumulator, R
  didn't track it at all — so the two implementations diverged in both structure
  and fidelity. Now both consume the same client report through mirrored
  `HistoryController` logic (a reported-messages read, a `ui_offset` cursor, and
  the same heuristic for attaching UI messages to the record). Fixes and
  behavior port directly across languages, and keeping the two in parity is much
  easier.
- **Less server-side state to drift.** A single source of truth lets Python
  delete its duplicate ledger and the two replay-suppression flags that guarded
  save idempotency — fiddly bookkeeping that still missed partial mid-restore
  reports. The guard is now a plain count comparison.
- **Faithful by construction.** The record is whatever the browser rendered, so
  transformations are captured automatically instead of relying on every server
  code path to mirror them.


## Tests

New Playwright coverage for the client-authoritative behavior (`client_state/`)
and its interaction with history (`history_idempotent_save`,
`history_out_of_band`, `history_cross_session_deps`,
`history_ui_offset_after_restore`), plus expanded R `testthat` coverage for the
new store format and node/UI attachment logic.

title: fix(pkg-py): api reference namespace issue
feat: refine chat history trigger, drawer, and fill layout
description:
## Summary

A refinement pass over the multi-conversation history UI (shipped in #266), polishing the drawer chrome and tightening how it integrates with the surrounding layout. Purely front-end (JS/SCSS) plus the generated dist assets copied into both packages; the Python/R APIs are unchanged except for one internal container-style helper.

**Layout anchoring.** The history trigger and drawer are now direct children of `<shiny-chat-container>` and anchored to the full-width container, while a new `.shiny-chat-wrapper` holds the width-limited, centered chat column. The container stays `display: grid` (element-selector SCSS beats bslib's flex rule) so bslib's fill child-rules stay inert and the messages area still grows. The chat column width is driven by `--_chat-width` (default `min(680px, 100%)`); `data-history-placement="right"` mirrors the trigger + drawer to the right edge (pure CSS, settable via `chat_ui(**kwargs)`).

**Sidebar clearance.** In sidebar layouts the trigger no longer collides with sidebar controls: a JS overlap-nudge probes the trigger's leading edge and shifts it inward past any obstacle, re-running on resize, sidebar transitions, and drawer open/close. While the drawer is open over a collapsed same-side sidebar, the bslib collapse-toggle is hidden (it would otherwise paint over the drawer). The `min-height` floor is set at element specificity with the 400px default supplied by a zero-specificity `:where()` rule, so both `min-height` and `--_min-height` remain author-overridable.

**Drawer redesign.** `_history.scss` and `ChatHistoryDrawer.tsx` were rewritten to follow the repo's `_command-chip.scss` token idiom (public `--shiny-chat-history-*` → private `--_` → `--bs-*` fallback, with `light-dark()` + `color-mix()` tints for hover/active states). The drawer is now a flex column with a pinned header (title + close) and toprow (ghost "New" button + search), and a scrollable list of dense single-line rows. Unicode-glyph controls were replaced with inline SVG icons; the trigger icon is now clock-rewind (history) rather than a hamburger. New/search share height via toprow `align-items: stretch` and a shared border token; type hierarchy runs header > controls (0.875rem) > titles > meta. Initial focus lands on the dialog container, and Close is first in tab order (matches visual reading order, WCAG 2.4.3).

**Fill-padding transfer.** When a `fill` chat is the sole child of a padded bslib fillable container (sidebar main, `card()` body, `page_fillable`), the trigger/drawer would inherit that padding and sit inset from the parent edge. `ChatContainer` now climbs the single-child fillable chain to the first padded ancestor, zeroes its inline padding, and re-applies the captured value to the centered content column via a public `--shiny-chat-fill-padding` token — so the trigger/drawer sit flush with the parent's outer edge while messages/input keep equivalent breathing room.

## Verification

Run this app and open the history drawer (move the `chat_ui(...)` call between the marked spots to exercise each layout):

```python
from shiny import App, Inputs, Outputs, Session, ui
from shinychat import Chat, chat_ui


def app_ui(request: object) -> ui.Tag:
    return ui.page_sidebar(
        ui.sidebar("Sidebar content"),
        # (A) Chat inside a padded card body: trigger/drawer sit flush with the
        #     card edge while the card keeps its surrounding `main` padding.
        ui.card(
            ui.card_header("Chat with history", ui.input_dark_mode()),
            ui.card_body(
                chat_ui("chat", data_history_placement="right"),
                padding="64px",
            ),
        ),
        # (B) Move the same chat_ui(...) call here (drop the card) to put the
        #     chat directly in the sidebar `main`: trigger/drawer go flush with
        #     the main edge and the content column keeps the 24px padding.
        fillable=True,
    )


def server(input: Inputs, output: Outputs, session: Session) -> None:
    Chat(id="chat")  # attach any chatlas/ellmer client


app = App(app_ui, server)
```

Check:
- Full-width grid container with the chat column centered at 680px; scrim spans the whole container.
- `data_history_placement="right"` mirrors trigger + drawer to the right edge; dropping it (or setting `"left"`) mirrors them back left.
- The trigger clears the sidebar toggle, and the sidebar collapse-toggle hides while the drawer is open over a collapsed same-side sidebar.
- In both spots (A) and (B) the trigger/drawer are flush with the parent's outer edge while the content column keeps the parent's padding.

Automated: `cd js && npm run lint` (clean); 636 JS tests pass; `ruff` + `pyright` clean; R `chat`/`greeting` snapshot tests pass.

title: feat: editable messages and sibling navigation
description:
### What this PR does

You can now edit a message you already sent, instead of only being able to send a new one. Hover a user message and click the pencil icon to open an inline editor (pre-filled with the original text); press **Cmd/Ctrl+Enter** to save and resend, or **Escape** to cancel. Editing a message forks the conversation from that point — the old branch isn't lost, it's kept as a sibling. `‹ 1 / 2 ›`-style controls appear on any message with more than one version, letting you step back and forth between them at any time, including after reloading the page or returning from the history drawer.

This builds on top of the [multi-conversation history feature](https://github.com/posit-dev/shinychat/pull/266) in the parent branch — editing and branch navigation both go through the same persistence path as regular turns, so edits and the sibling you branched from are saved to the conversation store and are still there (and still navigable) the next time you open that conversation, not just for the rest of the current session.

---

### Reviewer guide: architectural decisions

This branch is stacked on `feat/chat-history` (#266) — only the diff introduced by the tip commit is new; everything else is already reviewed/merged there.

**1. The tree schema stops being inert**

`feat/chat-history` deliberately built `ConversationRecord` as a tree of `ConversationNode`s "solely to support future message editing without a schema migration," while noting the branching machinery was inert — no sibling-creation path, no branch-selection UI. This PR is that future: `UpdateSiblingsAction`, `HistoryController.handle_edit` / `handle_navigate`, and the new tree-query helpers (`siblings_of`, `subtree_leaf`, `path_sibling_metadata`, `node_id_for_message_index`) are what actually walk the tree instead of treating it as a list.

**2. How editing forks a branch**

`handle_edit` doesn't create the sibling node itself — it rewinds `current_leaf` to the edited message's parent and replays the UI up to that point. The sibling is created implicitly when the resubmitted content flows back through the normal `on_response` save path (append-to-`current_leaf`), the same path a brand-new turn takes. The comment in `_history.py` around `handle_edit` calls this out explicitly, since it's easy to assume `handle_edit` does the branching directly.

**3. Navigation persists immediately, edits persist on response**

`handle_navigate` calls `store.put()` itself, since switching the active sibling doesn't otherwise trigger a save. `handle_edit` relies on the existing save-on-response effect, since the fork isn't "real" until the resubmitted turn actually completes.

**4. Sibling metadata is a side channel, not part of the message payload**

`_send_sibling_metadata` walks `path_node_ids()` and maps each node to a UI message index, sending an `update_siblings` transport action keyed by index rather than embedding position/count in the message data itself. Worth checking that this stays in sync with `ui_offset` and replay logic if either changes later.

title: fix(pkg-py): cancel button broken when Chat is inside a Shiny module
description:
## What broke

The stop/cancel button had no effect when `Chat` was used inside a Shiny module. Clicking it appeared to work visually, but the `StreamController` was never actually cancelled — the streaming response continued to completion.

## Root cause

`Chat._setup_client` constructs the cancel input ID as `f"{self.id}_cancel"`. `self.id` is a `ResolvedId` (e.g. `"foo-chat"`), but string interpolation strips that type, producing a plain string. When `session.input[plain_string]` is called inside a module session, Shiny tries to apply the module namespace prefix — which both rejects the hyphen in the already-resolved ID (raising `ValueError`) and would double-namespace it even if it didn't.

## Fix

Wrap with `ResolvedId(...)`, matching the pattern already used for `user_input_id` and `_slash_command_id` just above in `__init__`.

## Test

Added `auto_cancel_module` Playwright test that verifies the cancel button fires the `StreamController` when the chat lives inside a module. Confirmed red without the fix, green with it.

title: feat: multi-conversation history — drawer UI, pluggable stores, and restore modes (Python + R)
description:
This PR makes so apps that use ellmer/chatlas now get multi-conversation history automatically. More precisely, if you pass a `client=` to `Chat()` in Python, or supply a client to `chat_server()` in R, the history drawer appears without any extra wiring — a toggle icon opens a panel showing all past conversations, a New Chat button, LLM-generated titles, search, rename, and delete. Conversations are persisted per-user and survive redeployments on Posit Connect.

To opt out: pass `history=False` (Python) or `history=FALSE` (R). For apps that can't use the module pattern, `chat_enable_history()` (R) or `chat.history.enable()` (Python) lets you wire history manually.

### Restore mode

The most important option to know about is `restore_mode`, which controls how the active conversation is remembered across page reloads:

- **`"browser"` (default):** the active conversation ID is kept in `localStorage`. The URL doesn't change, but reloading the page returns the user to where they left off.
- **`"url"`:** the active conversation ID is stored as a plain `?shinychat_conversation_id=<id>` query parameter. The address bar updates in place (via `history.replaceState`) on each conversation switch — no page reload, no server bookmark configuration required. Use this if you want the URL to reflect the current conversation so users can share or bookmark a specific conversation.
- **`"bookmark"`:** fully participates in Shiny server bookmarking. After every LLM response, a fresh server bookmark is minted and the address bar updates to `?_state_id_=...`. On in-session conversation switches the controller navigates to the target conversation's bookmark URL (if one exists). Requires `bookmark_store="server"` in the Shiny app. Use this when the app already uses Shiny bookmarks to capture full input state alongside the chat — the conversation and the bookmark state stay in lockstep.
- **`"none"`:** no cross-session restore; every page load starts fresh.

One important nuance: switching conversations — whether triggered by a page load or a mid-session drawer click — restores the transcript and any per-conversation values captured by `on_save`, but does **not** automatically reset raw Shiny input controls like sliders or text boxes. Use `on_restore` callbacks to sync those explicitly.

**Passive Shiny bookmark integration.** Regardless of `restore_mode`, if the app has `bookmark_store="server"` configured, the history system automatically stamps the active conversation ID into any Shiny bookmark the user triggers. Reloading from such a bookmark reopens the correct conversation, even if `restore_mode` is `"browser"` or `"none"`. This is distinct from `restore_mode="bookmark"` above, which *actively mints* bookmarks — this passive integration just ensures that developer- or user-triggered bookmarks capture the current conversation.

### Storage and identity

History is stored server-side, scoped by user (or a custom scope), stored in memory (in devmode) or the filesystem. On Posit Connect the correct persistent directory is picked up automatically. You can configure where and how conversations are stored — in memory, the filesystem, or with a completely custom `ConversationStore` backend — as well as how users are identified and how conversation titles are generated.

**Scope / user identity.** On authenticated deployments (Posit Connect with auth enabled), `session.user` is used as the scope key, so each user sees only their own conversations. For unauthenticated sessions — local dev, public deployments — there is no server-side identity, so the history system mints a random token and stores it in the browser's `localStorage`. That token becomes the scope key: the same browser gets the same history across reloads, but a different browser (or a cleared `localStorage`) starts fresh and cannot see the previous conversations. The scope can also be set to a custom string or callable via `HistoryOptions(scope=...)` / `history_options(scope = ...)` — for example to share history across a group, or to hard-code a fixed scope during development.

**Storage quota.** Each user's history is capped at 100 MB by default (`max_store_mb=100` in `HistoryOptions` / `history_options()`). After every save, if the total size for that scope exceeds the cap, the oldest conversations (by `updated_at`) are evicted one at a time until usage falls back under the limit. The active conversation is never evicted mid-session. The cap can be raised, lowered, or removed entirely (`max_store_mb=None` in Python / `max_store_mb = NULL` in R) via the options object.

### Saving app state per conversation (advanced)

For apps where other parts of the UI are tightly coupled to the chat — a selected data source, a filter panel, a chosen model — you can attach extra state to each conversation that travels with it on save and restore. This is a niche use case: most apps won't need it. But for the ones that do, it works even if you're not using full Shiny bookmarking:

**Python:**
```python
@chat.history.on_save
def _(values):
    values["tab"] = input.tab()

@chat.history.on_restore
def _(values):
    ui.update_navs("tabs", selected=values.get("tab"))
```

**R**:
```r
mod <- chat_mod_server("chat", client = llm)

mod$history$on_save(\(values) { values$tab <- input$tab; values })
mod$history$on_restore(\(values) updateTabsetPanel(session, "tabs", selected = values$tab))
```

This is independent of Shiny's bookmark system — apps that wire `onBookmark` / `on_bookmark` handlers for their own purposes are not automatically bridged into per-conversation history state.

---

## Reviewer guide: architectural decisions

The history feature is built on a small number of load-bearing decisions. Understanding why each choice was made is the fastest way to build an accurate mental model of how the pieces fit together.

### 1. In-session swap, not URL-per-conversation

The most consequential design decision is that switching conversations is **not** a page reload. When the user clicks a conversation in the drawer, the controller:

1. Fetches the target `ConversationRecord` from the store
2. Replaces the LLM client's turn history via `adapter.set_turns_json()`
3. Runs `on_restore` callbacks with the conversation's saved `values` dict
4. Sends a `history_navigate` transport message — the JS replaces the rendered message list in place

The alternative — encoding each conversation as a bookmarked URL and navigating to it on switch — was rejected because every switch would require a full page reload, bookmarks aren't enumerable per user so you can't list them in a drawer, and URL-store apps and Shinylive would be out of reach entirely. The in-session swap is what makes a responsive drawer UI possible, but it comes with trade-offs that surface repeatedly in the implementation: app state restoration is partial (no input control reset mid-session), the JS `clear` action must be overridden to carry history state forward rather than wiping it, and a phantom-save guard is needed to prevent replaying a transcript from triggering a spurious write (see below).

### 2. The conversation record: a linear chain inside a tree schema

Each conversation is stored as a `ConversationRecord` — a tree of `ConversationNode` objects where every node holds one turn and a reference to its parent. Today all conversations are strictly linear: each new turn appends to `current_leaf`, and `path_node_ids()` (root → `current_leaf`) is the canonical turn sequence.

The tree shape exists solely to support future message editing without a schema migration: a re-sent message would create a sibling node branching off the parent rather than rewriting history. That machinery is currently inert — there's no sibling-creation code path, no branch-selection UI — but the schema is already capable of representing it.

For the purposes of code review and maintenance: treat the record as a list. Any code that walks `path_node_ids()` is just iterating turns in order. The `nodes` dict and parent-pointer fields are there for the future.

### 3. Pluggable store with Connect-aware default

`ConversationStore` is a five-method interface: `list()` (metadata only, no turns), `get()` (full record), `put()` (upsert), `delete()` (remove by id), and `total_size()` (bytes used by scope). All conversation I/O flows through this boundary, which is what makes swapping backends possible. The store is intentionally kept narrow — it knows nothing about users, sessions, or Shiny; it just reads and writes records keyed by `(scope, conversation_id)`.

The Connect persistence story is worth understanding explicitly. App working directories on Posit Connect are wiped on every redeploy, so writing to a path relative to the app is not safe. The default `FileConversationStore` uses `resolve_history_dir()` to discover a safe location at runtime, checking in priority order: `CONNECT_CONTENT_DATA_DIR` (an Early Access env var) → Shiny's bookmark save directory piggybacked via a reserved ID (`shinychat-conversations`) → `.shinychat/conversations` relative to the working directory as a local fallback. The bookmark save directory route is what makes this redeploy-safe on current Connect without the Early Access flag; the piggybacking via a reserved bookmark ID is a deliberate hack with a comment pointing to it.

### 4. Per-conversation app state via `on_save` / `on_restore`

When a conversation is saved, the controller invokes all callbacks registered with `@chat.history.on_save` (Python) or `mod$history$on_save()` (R), which write into a `values` dict that is stored alongside the turns. On restore, the corresponding `on_restore` callbacks receive that dict back. "Restore" means both page-load restore (when `restore_mode` is `"browser"` or `"url"` and a prior conversation is found) and in-session conversation switches — the same callbacks fire in both cases.

This is the public API for keeping auxiliary UI state — a selected model, an active tab, a filter panel — in sync with the active conversation. Raw Shiny input values are not synced automatically; `on_restore` is where you call `ui.update_*()` / `updateXxx()` to apply them.

The only remaining private Shiny API access is in `_history_store.py` (`shiny.bookmark._global.get_bookmark_save_dir_fn`) used by `resolve_history_dir()` to locate a redeploy-safe persistence path on Posit Connect. If Shiny ever ships a public equivalent, that is the only file that needs to change.

### 5. `restore_mode` covers two separate concerns

`restore_mode` looks like a single dial but it actually governs two independent mechanisms:

**Cross-reload persistence** — which conversation to reopen when the page loads fresh. `"browser"` stores the active conversation ID in `localStorage`; `"url"` stores it as a `?shinychat_conversation_id=<id>` query parameter and updates the address bar via `history.replaceState` on each response; `"bookmark"` actively mints a server bookmark after every response, keeping `?_state_id_=...` in sync and enabling full Shiny bookmark restore on page reload (requires `bookmark_store="server"`); `"none"` skips cross-reload tracking entirely.

**Per-conversation app state** — the `values` dict captured by `on_save`/`on_restore`. This always runs when a conversation is loaded, regardless of `restore_mode`. It is not controlled by `restore_mode` at all.

None of these modes automatically reset raw Shiny input controls. Apps that want input values to follow the active conversation must do so explicitly via `on_restore` — including `"bookmark"` mode, which handles bookmark *persistence* but not input *restoration*.

### 6. The phantom-save guard

Replaying a transcript on conversation switch works by calling `chat.append_message()` for each stored UI message. That's the same path a live response takes, and the same "on response complete" reactive fires. Without intervention, every conversation switch would immediately write a redundant save back to the store — and the diff between "turns I just loaded" and "turns as persisted" is empty, so the save would be harmless but wasteful and could mask real bugs.

The fix is `_suppress_next_save` (Python) and its R equivalent: a flag set just before replay begins that causes the save-on-response effect to swallow exactly one save. It self-heals: if the flag is incorrectly set and a genuine save is suppressed, the next response will re-diff and catch up correctly. This is one of the subtler pieces of state in the controller and the most likely place to look if you see a conversation switch that appears to save stale content.

title: feat!(pkg-r): add `chat_server()`, deprecate `chat_mod_server()` and `chat_mod_ui()`
description:
## Summary

`chat_server()` replaces `chat_mod_server()` as the primary way to wire up server-side chat logic.

The original module-based API (`chat_mod_ui()` / `chat_mod_server()`) was more structure than the use case needs. The goal of this API is simple: you hand us an ellmer client and we hook up all the server logic most people want — streaming, cancellation, bookmarking, etc. A full `moduleServer()` scope isn't required to deliver that. Furthermore, since part of the ID namespace is private/implicit, downstream logic that depends on the chat's ID (e.g., slash command JS events) need workarounds to work in the way users might expect. This change also better aligns the R package with the Python API where no modules are needed to get the "batteries included" experience. 

`chat_server()` does the same job but runs directly in the caller's session scope. If you're already inside a `moduleServer()`, you pass that session in — no extra nesting, no doubled namespaces.

## What changed

- **`chat_server(id, client, ..., session)`** — new exported function with the same logic as `chat_mod_server()`, but runs in the provided session scope rather than creating its own. Takes an explicit `session` parameter (defaults to `getDefaultReactiveDomain()`).
- **`chat_mod_server()`** — soft-deprecated (`0.5.0`). Now a thin wrapper around `chat_server()`.
- **`chat_mod_ui()`** — soft-deprecated (`0.5.0`). Replace with `chat_ui(NS(id, "chat"), ...)` in your module UI.

## Migration

The simplest case — no module needed at all:

```r
# Before (forced you into a module)
ui <- fluidPage(chat_mod_ui("chat"))
server <- function(input, output, session) {
  chat_mod_server("chat", client)
}

# After
ui <- fluidPage(chat_ui("chat"))
server <- function(input, output, session) {
  chat_server("chat", client)
}
```

If you're embedding chat inside an existing module, pass that module's `session` explicitly:

```r
ui <- function(id) {
  ns <- NS(id)
  chat_ui(ns("chat"))
}
server <- function(id, client) {
  shiny::moduleServer(id, function(input, output, session) {
    chat_server("chat", client, session = session)
  })
}
```

Existing code using `chat_mod_server()` continues to work with a deprecation notice.

title: refactor: rename chat_greeting() dismissible to persistent
description:
Closes #260

## Summary

Renames the `dismissible` parameter on `chat_greeting()` to `persistent` across the JS client, Python package, and R package. The old name implied a user-controlled close button that never existed — dismissal is entirely automatic. `persistent` is unambiguous: `persistent = FALSE` (the default) means the greeting hides on first activity; `persistent = TRUE` keeps it visible throughout the conversation.

**Polarity is inverted from the old default:** `dismissible = TRUE` (hide) → `persistent = FALSE` (hide); `dismissible = FALSE` (stay) → `persistent = TRUE` (stay).

Both R and Python include deprecation shims so existing code using `dismissible` warns rather than breaks. In R, `lifecycle::deprecate_warn("0.4.1", ...)` is used with `lifecycle::deprecated()` as the sentinel default; in Python, the project's existing `DEPRECATED`/`DEPRECATED_TYPE` sentinel pattern is used. Both `persistent` and `dismissible` are placed after `...`/`*` so they must be passed by name — positional calls will error with a clear message.

The wire format key sent from R/Python to the JS component also changes from `"dismissible"` to `"persistent"`.

## Verification

```r
library(shinychat)

# Default: greeting hides after first message (unchanged behavior)
chat_greeting("## Welcome!")

# Persistent: stays visible throughout
chat_greeting("Please read our terms.", persistent = TRUE)

# Old code: warns and maps correctly
chat_greeting("Please read our terms.", dismissible = FALSE)
#> Warning: `chat_greeting(dismissible)` was deprecated in shinychat 0.4.1.
#> Use `chat_greeting(persistent)` instead.
```

title: fix: exclude control inputs from Shiny bookmarking in chat_app()
description:
Fixes #258

## Summary
`chat_app()` and the underlying `chat_restore()` / `enable_bookmarking()` infrastructure were only excluding `{id}_user_input` from Shiny's bookmark state. Several control-only inputs could accidentally leak into the bookmarked URL or server-side state: the close button (`close_btn`) in `chat_app()`, the cancel/stop button (`{id}_cancel`), slash command triggers (`{id}_slash_command`), and the greeting-requested signal (`{id}_greeting_requested`).

The fix adds those four inputs to the exclusion list in all three relevant locations: `chat_restore.R` (R), `chat_app.R` (R), and `_chat.py` (Python).

## Verification
Run a `chat_app()` with `bookmark_store = "url"` and interact with the close button, cancel button, or a slash command. The resulting bookmark URL should contain only the conversation state — not any of those control input values.

title: fix: don't reserve space for attach button when upload is disabled
description:
## Problem

When `allow_attachments` is not set (the default), the chat input was still reserving `padding-left: 36px` on the text field — the same space used by the attach button when uploads *are* enabled. This left a visible gap on the left side of the input with no button to fill it.

Closes #256

## Fix

The unconditional `padding-left: 36px` on `.tiptap` is replaced with a `:has(.shiny-chat-btn-attach)` rule, so left padding is only applied when the attach button is actually rendered in the DOM.

Also removes the dead `textarea` rule inside `.shiny-chat-input` — `textarea` was replaced by Tiptap in #251 and the CSS was never cleaned up.

title: fix: prevent suggestion cards from overflowing in narrow sidebars
description:
The greeting / suggestion-cards feature could overflow the chat area in narrow containers such as Shiny sidebars, pushing cards past the visible edge.

## Cause

The suggestion-card grid uses an auto-fit track (`repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(175px, 100%), 1fr))`). Its max-content width propagated up the messages/greeting subtree because the grid item defaulted to `min-width: auto`, sizing the chat content to its content width rather than the available container width.

## Fix

Add `min-width: 0` to `.shiny-chat-messages-wrapper` so the grid child can shrink below its content size. Any residual scrollbar-gutter offset is absorbed by the wrapper's existing `overflow: clip`.

Verified across 250px / 350px / 500px container widths that the cards and greeting stay within the chat container.

title: fix: greeting state — bookmarking, dismissal observability, server readability
description:
Fixes #253

## Summary

Closes four gaps in greeting state management that made server-set greetings (`chat_set_greeting()` / `Chat.set_greeting()`) effectively write-only and ephemeral:

- **Gap 1 — Exclude `{id}_greeting_requested` from bookmarking** in both R and Python, matching the treatment of `{id}_user_input`. This is a state-derived signal, not persisted state.

- **Gap 4 — Observable dismissal** via a new `{id}_greeting_dismissed` Shiny input (integer event counter, `priority: "event"`). The JS effect fires when `greeting.status` transitions to `"dismissed"` and resets to `null` on `greeting_clear`. In R, `chat_get_greeting()` is the public getter for greeting content and dismissed status.

- **Gap 3 — Server-side readability** via `chat_get_greeting(id, session)` (R) and `chat.get_greeting()` (Python), returning the current greeting content and dismissed status. Internally, `chat_set_greeting()` writes to a session-keyed store; `chat_restore()` / `enable_bookmarking()` read from it.

- **Gap 2 — Auto-persist greeting through bookmark round-trips** — `chat_restore()` (R) and `enable_bookmarking()` (Python) now save and restore the greeting content transparently. A non-empty restored conversation correctly auto-dismisses the greeting via existing JS logic; an empty restore with a previously-dismissed greeting passes a `dismissed: true` flag on the wire action to suppress re-show.

- **Gap 5 — `ChatController` Playwright helpers** — adds `loc_greeting` property and `expect_greeting()` method to `pkg-py/src/shinychat/playwright/_chat.py`; migrates the greeting tests away from private module-level locator helpers.

## Verification

**R** — bookmark round-trips preserve the greeting, and dismissal is observable server-side:

```r
library(shiny)
library(shinychat)

client <- ellmer::chat_openai(model = "gpt-4o-mini")

ui <- function(req) {
  bslib::page_fillable(
    div(
      bookmarkButton(),
      actionButton("clear_chat", "Clear Chat")
    ),
    chat_ui("chat")
  )
}

server <- function(input, output, session) {
  chat_restore("chat", client)

  greetings <- c(
    "Hello! How can I help you?",
    "Hi there! What can I do for you today?",
    "Welcome! How can I assist you?"
  )

  chat_set_greeting("chat", sample(greetings, 1))

  observeEvent(input$chat_greeting_dismissed, {
    cat("Greeting dismissed at", input$chat_greeting_dismissed, "\n")
  })

  observeEvent(input$chat_user_input, {
    chat_append("chat", sprintf("You said: %s", input$chat_user_input))
  })

  observeEvent(input$clear_chat, {
    chat_clear("chat")
  })
}

shinyApp(ui, server, enableBookmarking = "url")
```

Bookmark the URL and reload — the greeting reappears (content persisted across the round-trip, even though `sample()` would otherwise pick a different message). Dismiss it; the server logs the timestamp.

**Python** — equivalent via `Chat.enable_bookmarking()` and `Chat.get_greeting()`.

description:
## Why this matters Users expect to be able to share images, documents, and code files in a chat — it's a standard interaction in ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and every other modern chat UI. Until now, shinychat only accepted plain text input, so developers who wanted multimodal input had to build their own file upload plumbing: drag-and-drop handling, MIME validation, base64 encoding, size limits, thumbnail previews, and conversion to the right LLM content types. This PR makes all of that built-in, so enabling file attachments is a one-liner. ## What it looks like Users can attach files via three input methods: the **+** button, **drag-and-drop**, or **clipboard paste**. ### Staging area (before sending) ### Sent message (in conversation) Attachments appear as compact badges above the message text in the user bubble — image thumbnails stay visual, text files show a snippet. ## How to use it ### Python — with `client=` (zero config) When a chatlas client is provided, attachments are enabled automatically — no extra code needed: ```python from chatlas import ChatAnthropic from shiny.express import ui from shinychat.express import Chat ui.page_opts(fillable=True) chat = Chat(id="chat", client=ChatAnthropic()) chat.ui() ``` ### R — with `chat_mod_server()` (zero config) ```r library(shinychat) library(ellmer) ui <- bslib::page_fillable(chat_mod_ui("chat")) server <- function(input, output, session) { chat <- chat_anthropic(system_prompt = "You are a helpful assistant.") chat_mod_server("chat", client = chat) } shinyApp(ui, server) ```
Manual wiring (Python) For custom LLM integrations, enable the UI and accept a second parameter in the submit handler: ```python from shinychat import Attachment, attachment_to_content from shinychat.express import Chat chat = Chat(id="chat") chat.ui(allow_attachments=True) @chat.on_user_submit async def handle(user_input: str, attachments: list[Attachment]): contents = [attachment_to_content(a) for a in attachments] response = await my_client.stream_async(user_input, *contents) await chat.append_message_stream(response) ```
Manual wiring (R) ```r ui <- bslib::page_fillable( chat_ui("chat", allow_attachments = TRUE) ) server <- function(input, output, session) { chat <- ellmer::chat_openai() observeEvent(input$chat_user_input, { # When attachments are enabled, input is a list of Content objects — # splice with !!! to pass them as individual arguments stream <- chat$stream_async(!!!input$chat_user_input) chat_append("chat", stream) }) } shinyApp(ui, server) ```
## Breaking changes ### R - When the user attaches files, `input$_user_input` changes from a plain character string to a list of ellmer `Content` objects. Splice either form to a chat method with `!!!` (e.g., `chat$stream_async(!!!input$_user_input)`) - `chat_mod_server()`'s `last_input` reactive mirrors this shape: string when attachments are disabled, list of `Content` objects when enabled. ### Python - `Chat.user_input()` no longer returns a plain string. It now returns `None` before the first submission, and a `UserInput` named tuple (`text`, `attachments`) after submission. - This is a breaking change for code that treated `chat.user_input()` as a `str`, or that assumed the previous return shape without a `None` check. ### Programmatic staging with `update_user_input()` Server-side code can now pre-populate attachments in the chat input — useful for seeding context from a database, prior conversation, or a user action elsewhere in the app: **Python** ```python att = Attachment.from_path("report.pdf") chat.update_user_input( value="Summarize this report", attachments=[att], submit=True, # optional: auto-send immediately ) ``` **R** ```r att <- chat_attachment("report.pdf") update_chat_user_input( "chat", value = "Summarize this report", attachments = list(att), submit = TRUE ) ``` `attachment_mode` controls how new attachments combine with any already-staged files: `"append"` (default) adds to the set, `"set"` replaces it. Pass `attachments=[]` with `attachment_mode="set"` to clear. ## Supported file types | Family | Types | Behavior | |--------|-------|----------| | **Images** | PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP | Thumbnail preview; large images auto-downscaled to 1568px longest edge | | **PDF** | PDF | Document badge with filename | | **Text/code** | `.md`, `.txt`, `.csv`, `.json`, `.py`, `.js`, `.ts`, `.r`, `.yaml`, `.toml`, `.qmd`, `.rmd`, `.sql`, `.sh`, `.html`, `.css`, `.xml`, and more | Content preview card showing first few lines of the file | This is the initial supported set — it can grow as [chatlas](https://github.com/posit-dev/chatlas) and [ellmer](https://github.com/tidyverse/ellmer) add support for additional file types. Max combined size defaults to **30 MB**, configurable via the `SHINYCHAT_MAX_ATTACHMENT_SIZE` environment variable. ## Notable behaviors - **Image downscaling**: Images larger than 1568px on their longest edge are automatically downscaled client-side before sending, matching Anthropic's recommended input size. - **Long paste → attachment**: Clipboard pastes over 1000 characters are automatically converted into a "Pasted Text" file attachment instead of flooding the textarea. - **Animated GIF → still**: GIFs are converted to a still frame (with a notice) since most LLM APIs don't support animation. - **Bookmarking**: Attachment state is included in bookmark/restore — user messages with attachments round-trip correctly. ## Reviewer notes The implementation is layered across three commits, one per package: 1. **`js/`** — Attachment staging UI (React), file processing pipeline (downscaling, MIME resolution, size validation), and the `setInputValue` extension for programmatic staging. All client-side; no new dependencies. 2. **`pkg-py/`** — `Attachment` Pydantic model with `from_path()`/`from_data()`/`from_url()` constructors, `attachment_to_content()` converter to chatlas types, `InputHandler` for automatic argument injection on `@on_user_submit`, and `allow_attachments` parameter on `chat_ui()`. 3. **`pkg-r/`** — `chat_attachment()` constructor, `resolve_attachment_attrs()` for MIME validation, `allow_attachments` on `chat_ui()` / `chat_app()`, and server-side deserialization into ellmer `Content` objects. The canonical list of supported MIME types lives in `js/src/chat/attachment-types.json` and is copied to both packages at build time — Python and R read it at load time to stay in sync with the client.

title: chore(pkg-py): migrate storage-layer types from TypedDicts/dataclasses to Pydantic models
description:
## Summary

The internal types that represent stored chat messages and their content segments (`StoredMessage`, content segments, etc.) were a mix of `TypedDict`s and `@dataclass`es. This worked, but it meant bookmark serialization/deserialization was hand-rolled, dict-style field access (`s["content"]`) was used in some places and attribute access (`s.content`) in others, and there was no validation on data coming in from bookmarks.

This PR migrates those storage-layer types to Pydantic `BaseModel`s.

## What improves

- **Bookmark restore is validated.** Restoring a bookmarked message now goes through `StoredMessage.model_validate()`, so malformed or incompatible bookmark data raises a clear Pydantic `ValidationError` (chained for diagnostics) instead of blowing up at an arbitrary point downstream.
- **Bookmark serialization is `model_dump()`.** The old `BookmarkMessageDict` TypedDict and its manual construction are gone — `StoredMessage` knows how to serialize itself.
- **Uniform attribute access.** Segments are now always accessed as `s.content`, `s.content_type`, `s.html_deps` — no more mixed dict/attribute styles.
- **`SerializedDep` type alias.** `dict[str, object]` appeared in ~8 signatures to represent a serialized HTML dependency. It now has a name (`SerializedDep`), making intent clearer and grep-able.
- **Cleaner segment type hierarchy.** A `_SegmentBase` model holds the shared fields (`content`, `content_type`) and the `stringify` logic. `ContentSegment` (live, holds `HTMLDependency` objects) and `StoredSegment` (serialized, holds `SerializedDep` dicts) both inherit from it, differing only in their `html_deps` type.
- **`wire_segments()` method.** The inline dict-comprehension that built `MessagePayloadSegment` lists for the wire format now lives on `StoredMessage` where it belongs.

## What doesn't change

- Wire format to the JS client is identical.
- `ChatMessage`, `ChatGreeting`, and all the `ChatAction` TypedDicts are untouched — this only affects the *storage* layer.
- No new dependencies (`pydantic` is already a transitive dep via Shiny).

title: feat: segment-based message storage (mixed content + thinking)
description:
## Why

> *(scope note: the motivating problem and the substantive fix are Python-side. R and JS get a wire-protocol update for parity, but no R user-facing behavior changes here.)*

In **Shiny for Python**, bookmarking a streamed assistant reply that mixed content types — markdown, a raw-HTML widget (with its `HTMLDependency`), and reasoning — used to lose type and dependency information on restore: the message came back flattened, styling and structure gone. This reworks how messages are represented so those replies round-trip faithfully, and folds model "thinking" into the same model instead of the previous `<thinking>`-tag string workaround.

## What changed

The core shift is from a **single-string** content model to a list of **typed segments**.

- **Before:** a message was one `content` string + one `content_type`. Thinking was smuggled in by wrapping text in `<thinking>…</thinking>` inside the markdown string, then re-parsed on the client. A reply couldn't faithfully represent "markdown, then an HTML widget, then reasoning" — it all collapsed to one type.
- **After:** a message is an ordered list of `{content, content_type}` segments, where `content_type ∈ markdown | html | text | thinking`. Adjacent same-type chunks merge; a type change opens a new segment. Thinking is a first-class segment type rather than a tag convention.

Segments back server-side storage, bookmarks, and the complete-message wire payload (the `message` action). Streaming stays delta-based: an empty segment-shaped `chunk_start` (carrying role/icon) is followed by flat `chunk` deltas, each a single content type, which the client reassembles into its render model; greetings remain flat too. The **Python** side (`StoredMessage`, segment serialize/restore) is where mixed-content replies are now preserved end to end. **R** emits the same payload shapes for parity (always a single segment today), and the **JS** client materializes segments at ingest — but neither gains new storage behavior.

## What's now possible

- A single streamed message can interleave **markdown + HTML + thinking** and survive a bookmark round-trip intact — content types preserved, HTML dependencies (CSS/JS) re-applied. Covered by a new Playwright end-to-end test.
- **Thinking is a first-class content segment.** Structured reasoning (chatlas / ellmer `ContentThinking`) and raw inline `<thinking>` tags both render through the existing thinking panel.

## Approach notes

On the JS client, `main`'s richer **`blocks`** render model — the streaming thinking-tag state machine, topic labels, duration timer, and code-fence handling — is **preserved unchanged** and derived from segments at ingest. (A pure render-time derivation couldn't reproduce the cross-chunk streaming state, so the reducer stays authoritative for live rendering, while segments own storage and the complete-message payload.) The old `<thinking>`-tag buffering hack in `_append_message_stream` is removed.

**Breaking:** bookmark restore assumes segments are present — there's no legacy fallback, so bookmarks written by an earlier version will fail to restore rather than degrade.

## Testing

- JS: 454 vitest tests pass; lint clean
- Python: 87 unit tests pass; pyright 0 errors; ruff clean
- R: 186 testthat tests pass
- New Playwright e2e: mixed markdown + thinking + HTML bookmark round-trip

---

This likely supersedes #213, which targeted the same problem before `main` gained thinking support.

fix: Preserve conversation when a chat is moved in the DOM (#121)
description:
## Why this matters

Moving a `chat_ui()` element to a different DOM container currently **wipes its rendered conversation** — the greeting, message history, and any streamed replies all vanish, and the input can end up in a broken state.

This blocks real use cases where a chat lives inside a larger component that gets relocated. The motivating example ([blockr.ui#106](https://github.com/BristolMyersSquibb/blockr.ui/issues/106)): AI-assistant chats embedded in canvas "blocks" that are moved to a hidden holding area when a block is closed and moved back when it's reopened. After a move, the chat is empty.

This was originally reported and fixed in #121 / #122 (the Lit era), but the fix was **lost in the Lit→React migration** (#181). The same latent bug also affects `markdown_stream()`.

## Background: why moving the element destroys the conversation

Both `<shiny-chat-container>` and `<shiny-markdown-stream>` are custom elements that mount a React root into themselves. The conversation only exists as **React state** — the server-rendered `<shiny-chat-message>` tags are read once at boot (`parseInitialMessages`) and then replaced by React's own DOM; streamed messages are never written back to the DOM.

When you move a connected element with `appendChild`/`appendTo`, the browser fires `disconnectedCallback` and then `connectedCallback` **synchronously, in the same tick**. The old code did this:

- `disconnectedCallback()` → immediately `reactRoot.unmount()` (destroys all React state and removes its DOM)
- `connectedCallback()` → rebuild from scratch; `parseInitialMessages()` now finds no `<shiny-chat-message>` tags → empty conversation

So a move tears the conversation down and rebuilds it empty. (For `markdown_stream()` the *initial* `content` attribute is re-read on reconnect, so only **streamed** content is lost — still a bug.)

## The fix

**Defer the teardown instead of running it synchronously**, and cancel it if the element reconnects in the same tick:

- `disconnectedCallback()` schedules teardown via `setTimeout(…, 0)` rather than unmounting immediately.
- `connectedCallback()` cancels any pending teardown at the top. Since a move fires disconnect→connect synchronously, the timer never gets a chance to run — the live React root (and its DOM, which the browser moves along with the element) stays intact. The existing `if (this.reactRoot) return` guard then short-circuits re-initialization.
- A **genuine** removal has no following reconnect to cancel the timer, so teardown runs on the next tick exactly as before — no leaks.

This works because moving a DOM node moves its entire subtree intact; React doesn't care where its container lives in the document. The only thing that was breaking us was throwing the root away and rebuilding, so the minimal correct fix is "don't throw it away during a move."

### Trade-offs considered

- **Why not serialize messages back to the DOM on disconnect and re-parse on reconnect?** Lossy and fragile — streamed content (tool calls, rich blocks, thinking, etc.) isn't representable as the simple `<shiny-chat-message content="…">` tags, and it would mean maintaining a second serialization path. Keeping the existing React tree alive preserves *everything* for free.
- **Why a deferred timer rather than detecting "is this a move?"** The platform gives no "moved" signal; disconnect/reconnect is the only observable. Deferring and cancelling is the standard, robust pattern for move-resilient custom elements, and it degrades correctly: a real removal still cleans up, just one tick later.
- **Cost:** a single pending `setTimeout(0)` per disconnect; negligible.

The same pattern is applied to both `chat-entry.ts` and `markdown-stream-entry.ts` (kept parallel rather than abstracted into a shared base — there's no shared base class for these entry points and the teardown bodies differ).

## Tests

- **JS unit (`chat-entry.test.ts`):**
  - *preserves the rendered conversation when moved to another container* — asserts the message element is the **same DOM node** before/after the move (proving state was preserved, not re-parsed).
  - *tears down when genuinely removed (not moved)* — guards the deferred-cleanup path so a real removal still unbinds/unmounts.
- **JS unit (`markdown-stream-entry.test.ts`):** *preserves streamed content when moved* — streams content that lives only in React state (not the `content` attribute) and asserts it survives the move. The existing queue-clearing test was updated to reflect the now-deferred teardown timing (same behavioral contract).
- **Playwright e2e (`pkg-py/.../chat/move/`):** reproduces the issue's exact scenario — sends a message, moves `#chat` from one container to another client-side, and asserts the full conversation survives and the chat still works afterward. Confirmed this test **fails on the pre-fix build** and passes after.

Verified: full JS unit suite + lint green; representative existing Playwright tests (`basic`, `dynamic_ui`, `stream`, `message_stream_context`) still pass.

Fixes #121
